ideas.a: Hairs and mucus trap dust and germs from the air
It moistens the air and heats it to body temperature

model: The space behind your face where air first comes in: hairs and mucus trap dust, and the air is heated and moistened before it goes on.

ideas.a: It closes over the entrance to the trachea (the larynx)
This happens when you eat or drink, so nothing goes down the wrong way and you don't choke

model: A small piece of cartilage that closes over the top of the trachea when you eat or drink, so nothing goes down the wrong way.

ideas.a: It makes the sounds we talk and sing with
Cords (folds) inside it vibrate as air passes over them
It sits at the top of the trachea, below the pharynx

model: It sits at the top of the trachea; cords inside it vibrate as air passes over them, making the sounds we talk and sing with.

ideas.a: Stiff C-shaped hoops in its wall keep it open, so it does not collapse
It is lined with mucus and cilia, which trap dust and sweep it up
It carries air from the larynx down to the two bronchi

model: The main airway, from the larynx down to the bronchi: stiff C-shaped hoops stop it collapsing, and it is lined with mucus and cilia.

ideas.a: There are two of them, one going into each lung
Each one divides into smaller airways, the bronchioles
Like the trachea, they are held open by cartilage

model: The pair of airways, one going into each lung; cartilage holds them open, and inside the lung each one divides into bronchioles.

ideas.a: They carry air to the alveoli, where they end
They come off the bronchi, inside the lungs
Their walls have smooth muscle (but no cartilage)

model: Narrow airways inside the lungs that come off the bronchi and carry air to the alveoli; their walls have smooth muscle.

ideas.a: Oxygen diffuses from them into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses the other way
Their walls are very thin: only one cell thick
Each one is wrapped in a dense network of capillaries
There are millions of them, giving a huge surface area, and the inside is moist

model: Millions of tiny air pockets with walls one cell thick, wrapped in capillaries: oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out.

ideas.a: It separates the chest (thorax) from the abdomen, below the lungs
When you breathe in it contracts and moves down
When you breathe out it relaxes and rises back up

model: The wall between the chest and the abdomen: when you breathe in it contracts and moves down, and when you breathe out it relaxes and rises back up.

ideas.a: They lie in the gaps of the bony cage around the lungs
When you breathe in they contract and pull the chest up and out
They work with the diaphragm in breathing

model: Found in the gaps of the bony cage that protects the lungs; with the diaphragm they contract to pull that cage up and out when you breathe in.

ideas.a: It detects a rise in carbon dioxide in the blood (the blood becomes more acidic, its pH falls)
It sends nerve impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles
So breathing becomes faster and deeper
It is at the base of the skull, at the top of the spinal cord

model: At the top of the spinal cord: it detects a rise in carbon dioxide in the blood and sends impulses to the breathing muscles, so you breathe faster and deeper.

ideas.a: It picks up oxygen in the lungs (forming oxyhaemoglobin)
It is a protein pigment inside the erythrocytes
It lets go of the oxygen in the tissues, where oxygen is low

model: A protein pigment inside erythrocytes: it picks up oxygen in the lungs, where there is plenty, and releases it in the tissues, where oxygen is low.

ideas.a: Particles spread out from where there are many of them to where there are few
It is passive: it needs no energy
It is how oxygen passes from the alveoli into the blood (and carbon dioxide the other way)

model: Particles spreading out from where there are many to where there are few, with no energy needed; it is how oxygen gets from the alveoli into the blood.

ideas.a: The diaphragm contracts and flattens (moves down)
The intercostal muscles contract and the rib cage moves up and out
The chest (thoracic cavity) gets bigger, so the pressure inside falls and air is drawn in

model: The diaphragm contracts and flattens and the rib cage moves up and out, so the chest gets bigger and the pressure inside it drops.

ideas.a: The diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, and the diaphragm domes back up
The rib cage moves down and in
The chest gets smaller, so the pressure inside rises and air is pushed out

model: The diaphragm and the muscles between the ribs relax: the diaphragm domes again, the rib cage sinks back in, the chest gets smaller and the pressure inside rises.

ideas.a: Tiny threads on the cells lining the trachea and bronchi
They move the sticky layer up to the throat, away from the lungs
This clears trapped dust and germs out of the airways

model: Tiny threads on the cells lining the trachea that wave to move sticky slime, with trapped dust and germs, up to the throat, away from the lungs.
